claim: Williams syndrome (WS; OMIM#194050) is a rare disorder with a prevalence of 1 in 7500 live births.
source: Williams syndrome, also known as Williams-Beuren syndrome (WS; OMIM#194050) is a rare disorder with a prevalence of 1 in 7500 live births (Kozel et al., 2021; Pober, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kozel et al., 2021; Pober, 2010).

claim: WS is caused by the microdeletion of approximately 25–27 genes on chromosome 7q11.23.
source: WS is caused by the microdeletion of approximately 25–27 genes (termed as WS genes) on chromosome 7q11.23 and affects multiple systems including cardiovascular and neuronal systems (Collins, 2013; Collins, 2018; Lin et al., 2019; Pober et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Collins, 2013; Collins, 2018; Lin et al., 2019; Pober et al., 2008).

claim: WS affects multiple systems including cardiovascular and neuronal systems.
source: WS is caused by the microdeletion of approximately 25–27 genes (termed as WS genes) on chromosome 7q11.23 and affects multiple systems including cardiovascular and neuronal systems (Collins, 2013; Collins, 2018; Lin et al., 2019; Pober et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Collins, 2013; Collins, 2018; Lin et al., 2019; Pober et al., 2008).

claim: Most individuals with WS displayed neuronal phenotypes including hypersociability, impaired myelination and intellectual disability (IQ <70).
source: Most individuals with WS displayed neuronal phenotypes including hypersociability, impaired myelination and intellectual disability (IQ <70; Barak and Feng, 2016; Barak et al., 2019; Kozel et al., 2021; Morris and Braddock, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Barak and Feng, 2016; Barak et al., 2019; Kozel et al., 2021; Morris and Braddock, 2020).

claim: fMRI neuroimaging and examination with post-mortem brain tissues of WS patients both showed abnormalities of brain structure of WS patients, including visuospatial construction deficit and increased length of dendrites, numbers of spine and branching points.
source: fMRI neuroimaging and examination with post-mortem brain tissues of WS patients both showed abnormalities of brain structure of WS patients, including visuospatial construction deficit and increased length of dendrites, numbers of spine and branching points (Chailangkarn et al., 2016; Kippenhan et al., 2005; Meyer-Lindenberg et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chailangkarn et al., 2016; Kippenhan et al., 2005; Meyer-Lindenberg et al., 2004).

claim: Neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and neurons derived from the induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) of WS patient display deficits, such as increased apoptosis, aberrant morphological complexity and electrophysiological activity.
source: Neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and neurons derived from the induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) of WS patient display deficits, such as increased apoptosis, aberrant morphological complexity and electrophysiological activity (Chailangkarn et al., 2016; Khattak et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chailangkarn et al., 2016; Khattak et al., 2015).

claim: Neuronal deletion of WS gene Gtf2i leads to severe behavioral deficits and reduced myelination in mice.
source: Neuronal deletion of WS gene Gtf2i leads to severe behavioral deficits and reduced myelination in mice (Barak et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Barak et al., 2019).

claim: GTF2IRD1, GTF2I, BAZ1B, VPS37D, STX1A, CLIP2, LIMK1, MLXIPL, and ELN could be the key genes for the phenotypes of WS.
source: Although single gene mutation of those 25–27 genes only causes partial phenotypes of WS, genotype-phenotype relationship analysis suggests that GTF2IRD1, GTF2I, BAZ1B, VPS37D, STX1A, CLIP2, LIMK1, MLXIPL, and ELN could be the key genes for the phenotypes (Kozel et al., 2021; Lek et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kozel et al., 2021; Lek et al., 2016).

claim: GTF2IRD1 encodes DNA binding protein of the Transcription factor (TF) II-I family.
source: GTF2IRD1 encodes DNA binding protein of the Transcription factor (TF) II-I family and its deficiency contributes to neurological deficits of WS patients, such as the impaired motor coordination, visual-spatial constructive deficits and cognitive deficits (Carmona-Mora et al., 2015; Corley et al., 2016; Dai et al., 2009; Enkhmandakh et al., 2009; Kopp et al., 2020; Makeyev and Bayarsaihan, 2009; Morris et al., 2003; O'Leary and Osborne, 2011; Tassabehji et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GTF2IRD1 deficiency contributes to neurological deficits of WS patients, such as the impaired motor coordination, visual-spatial constructive deficits and cognitive deficits.
source: GTF2IRD1 encodes DNA binding protein of the Transcription factor (TF) II-I family and its deficiency contributes to neurological deficits of WS patients, such as the impaired motor coordination, visual-spatial constructive deficits and cognitive deficits (Carmona-Mora et al., 2015; Corley et al., 2016; Dai et al., 2009; Enkhmandakh et al., 2009; Kopp et al., 2020; Makeyev and Bayarsaihan, 2009; Morris et al., 2003; O'Leary and Osborne, 2011; Tassabehji et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: WS forebrain organoids showed a higher percentage of KI67+/SOX2+ cells compared to that of CTRL organoids.
source: We first performed immunofluorescence staining and observed that WS forebrain organoids showed a higher percentage of KI67+/SOX2+ cells compared to that of CTRL organoids (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The percentage of EdU+/SOX2+ cells significantly increased in WS organoids.
source: Further, CTRL and WS organoids were pulsed with 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU) at a dosage of 10  μM for 2 hr, and we found that the percentage of EdU+/SOX2+ cells also significantly increased in WS organoids (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The percentage of Ki67-EdU+ cells was significantly decreased in WS organoids.
source: Furthermore, CTRL and WS organoids were incorporated with EdU for 24 hr, and the cell cycle exiting of neural progenitor cells (NPCs) was assessed by analyzing the co-localization of EdU and Ki67. We observed that the percentage of Ki67-EdU+ cells was significantly decreased in WS organoids (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU and Ki67 co-localization data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Fewer TBR2+ intermediate neural progenitor cells (IPCs) localized at MAP2- ventricular zone (VZ) like layer in WS forebrain organoids compared to the CTRL organoids.
source: Fewer TBR2+ intermediate neural progenitor cells (IPCs) localized at MAP2- ventricular zone (VZ) like layer in WS forebrain organoids compared to the CTRL organoids (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: The expression of neuronal precursor and immature neuronal cell marker doublecortin positive (DCX+) cells at SOX2+ ventricle (VZ)-like layer significantly decreased in WS forebrain organoids.
source: We found that upon the differentiation, the expression of neuronal precursor and immature neuronal cell marker doublecortin positive (DCX+) cells at SOX2+ ventricle (VZ)-like layer significantly decreased in WS forebrain organoids (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The relative thickness of the VZ layer indicated by SOX2+ aberrantly increased in WS forebrain organoids.
source: The relative thickness of the VZ layer indicated by SOX2+ aberrantly increased, but the thickness of cortical plate (CP) layer indicated by MAP2+ abnormally decreased (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The thickness of cortical plate (CP) layer indicated by MAP2+ abnormally decreased in WS forebrain organoids.
source: The relative thickness of the VZ layer indicated by SOX2+ aberrantly increased, but the thickness of cortical plate (CP) layer indicated by MAP2+ abnormally decreased (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The total number and the proportion of neuronal marker CTIP2+ cells in CP like layer were significantly decreased in WS forebrain organoids.
source: The total number (Figure 2F and G) and the proporation of neuronal marker CTIP2+ cells in CP like layer (Figure 2F and H) were significantly decreased in WS forebrain organoids.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2F, G, and H.

claim: The total number and the proportion of neuronal marker TBR1+ cells in CP like layer were significantly decreased in WS forebrain organoids.
source: The total number (Figure 2I and J) and the proporation of neuronal marker TBR1+ cells in CP like layer (Figure 2I and K) were also significantly decreased in WS forebrain organoids.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2I, J, and K.

claim: Bulk RNA-seq revealed 1761 differentially expressed genes (DEGs): 1003 down-regulated and 758 up-regulated in WS forebrain organoids.
source: In addition, RNA-seq data analysis revealed 1761 differentially expressed genes (DEGs): 1003 down-regulated and 758 up-regulated (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis with all DEG showed enrichment for neuronal development and neurogenesis.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis with all DEG showed enrichment for neuronal development and neurogenesis (Figure 3D), and interaction network of top 30 genes related to neurogenesis was shown (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: GO analysis revealed the enrichment of up-regulated genes for cell proliferation and of down-regulated genes for neuronal differentiation, synaptic signaling and neurogenesis.
source: GO analysis also revealed the enrichment of up-regulated genes for cell proliferation and of down-regulated genes for neuronal differentiation, synaptic signaling and neurogenesis (Figure 3F and G), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: The levels of SOX2, NESTIN, PAX6, and HES5 were significantly increased in WS organoids compared to CTRL.
source: WB assay and quantification results showed that the levels of SOX2, NESTIN, PAX6, and HES5 were significantly increased (Figure 3J–N) and the levels of TBR1, SATB2, and CTIP2 (Figure 3O–R) were significantly decreased in WS organoids compared to CTRL.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3J-N.

claim: The levels of TBR1, SATB2, and CTIP2 were significantly decreased in WS organoids compared to CTRL.
source: WB assay and quantification results showed that the levels of SOX2, NESTIN, PAX6, and HES5 were significantly increased (Figure 3J–N) and the levels of TBR1, SATB2, and CTIP2 (Figure 3O–R) were significantly decreased in WS organoids compared to CTRL.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3O-R.

claim: Total 96,969 cells were obtained from CTRL and WS samples for scRNA-seq analysis.
source: After quality control, total 96,969 cells were obtained from CTRL and WS samples, and were analyzed together using unsupervised clustering (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: UMAP identified 13 cell clusters in CTRL and WS forebrain organoids.
source: Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) identified 13 cell clusters in CTRL and WS forebrain organoids, which were then annotated using the expression of cell-type-specific markers (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The proportions of deeper layer_projection neuron (DL_PN) and upper layer projection neuron (UL_PN) clusters were significantly decreased in WS forebrain organoids compared to CTRL.
source: We observed that the proportions of deeper layer_projection neuron (DL_PN) and upper layer projection neuron (UL_PN) clusters were significantly decreased in WS forebrain organoids compared to CTRL, while the proportions of other clusters did not show significant difference between CTRL and WS organoids (Figure 4C–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: DL_PN and UL_PN were excitatory neurons according to the markers BCl11B and FEZF2.
source: According to the markers for the cluster characterization including BCl11B and FEZF2, DL_PN and UL_PN were excitatory neurons (Paulsen et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Paulsen et al., 2022) and marker expression.

claim: GO analysis with DEGs in DL_PN and UL_PN clusters showed the enrichment for neuronal development and neuronal differentiation.
source: GO analysis with DEGs in DL_PN and UL_PN clusters showed the enrichment for neuronal development and neuronal differentiation (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: The pesudotime of excitatory neuronal trajectories in WS organoids showed a remarkable delayed development compared to CTRL organoids.
source: The pesudotime of excitatory neuronal trajectories in WS organoids analysis showed a remarkable delayed development compared to CTRL organoids (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pseudotime analysis data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The excitatory neuronal lineage displayed an increased distribution towards the start point trajectory and a decreased distribution towards the end point trajectory in WS organoids.
source: Pseudotime uniform manifold approximation analysis revealed that the excitatory neuronal lineage displayed an increased distribution towards the start point trajectory and a decreased distribution towards the end point trajectory in WS organoids (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by pseudotime analysis data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The expression of NPC marker genes SOX2 and TBR2 exhibited increasing trend at early stage of trajectories in WS organoids.
source: Furthermore, the expression of NPC marker genes SOX2 and TBR2 exhibited increasing trend at early stage of trajectories, but the expression of neuronal marker genes NHLH1, TBR1, CTIP2, and SATB2 showed decreasing trend at middle and later stages of trajectories in WS organoids (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The expression of neuronal marker genes NHLH1, TBR1, CTIP2, and SATB2 showed decreasing trend at middle and later stages of trajectories in WS organoids.
source: Furthermore, the expression of NPC marker genes SOX2 and TBR2 exhibited increasing trend at early stage of trajectories, but the expression of neuronal marker genes NHLH1, TBR1, CTIP2, and SATB2 showed decreasing trend at middle and later stages of trajectories in WS organoids (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Integrated analysis with down-regulated genes identified both by bulk RNA-seq data and scRNA-seq revealed one overlapped gene transthyretin (TTR).
source: Integrated analysis with down-regulated genes identified both by bulk RNA-seq data and scRNA-seq, respectively, revealed one overlapped gene transthyretin (TTR; Figure 6A), whereas there is no overlapped genes were identified in up-regulated genes by bulk RNA-seq data and scRNA-seq, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by integrated analysis data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TTR is required for the transportation of thyroxine and retinol and plays an essential function in the development of the central nervous system.
source: TTR is required for the transportation of thyroxine and retinol and plays an essential function in the development of the central nervous system (Fleming et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2016; Magalhães et al., 2021; Santos et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Fleming et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2016; Magalhães et al., 2021; Santos et al., 2010).

claim: TTR was widely expressed in all cell clusters of CTRL organoids, but significantly decreased in WS organoids.
source: scRNA-seq data analysis showed that TTR was widely expressed in all cell clusters of CTRL organoids, but significantly decresaed in WS organoids (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining, qRT-PCR and WB assay results confirmed the remarkable decrease of TTR in WS brain organoids relative to Ctrl.
source: Immunofluorescence staining, qRT-PCR and WB assay results confirmed the remarkable decrease of TTR in WS brain organoids relative to Ctrl (Figure 6D–G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence, qRT-PCR, and Western blot data shown in Figure 6D-G.

claim: RNA-seq data analysis showed that down-regulated genes enriched for MAPK signaling pathway.
source: Of note, RNA-seq data anaylsis showed that down-regulated genes enriched for MAPK signaling pathway (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: WB assay results showed the significant reduction of GTF2IRD1 and p-ERK/ERK in WS brain organoids.
source: WB assay results showed the significant reduction of GTF2IRD1 and p-ERK/ERK in WS brain organoids (Figure 6I–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6I-L.

claim: The depletion of GTF2IRD1 but not GTF2I led to a significant decrease of TTR.
source: We observed that the depletion of GTF2IRD1 but not GTF2I led to a significant decrease of TTR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: TTR exposure significantly increased the level p-ERK in WS brain organoids.
source: WB assay and quantification results showed TTR exposure significantly increased the level p-ERK (Figure 7A–C), which could be significantly inhibited by the supplement of TTR inhibitor receptor-associated protein (RAP), a ligand inhibiting the internalization of TTR (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: The increase of p-ERK by TTR could be significantly inhibited by the supplement of TTR inhibitor receptor-associated protein (RAP).
source: WB assay and quantification results showed TTR exposure significantly increased the level p-ERK (Figure 7A–C), which could be significantly inhibited by the supplement of TTR inhibitor receptor-associated protein (RAP), a ligand inhibiting the internalization of TTR (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: TTR exposure remarkably enhanced the percentages of CTIP2+ cells compared to untreated WS organoids.
source: RAP Immunofluorescence staining and quantification results showed that both TTR exposure remarkably enhanced the percentages of CTIP2+ cells compared to untreated WS organoids (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 7G and H.

claim: TTR exposure significantly increased the percentages of TBR1+ cells.
source: TTR exposure also significantly increased the percentages of TBR1+ cells (Figure 7I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 7I and J.

claim: Gtf2ird1+/- and Gtf2ird1-/- mice had the increased BrdU+ neuronal progenitor cells in VZ/SVZ regions relative to WT mice.
source: Immunofluorescence staining with brain sections and quantification results showed that Gtf2ird1+/-and Gtf2ird1-/- mice had the increased BrdU+ (Figure 8A and B) and Ki67+Sox2+ (Figure 8C and D) neuronal progenitor cells in VZ/SVZ regions, respectively, but had the decreased CTIP2+ (Figure 8E and F), STAB+ cells (Figure 8E and G) and TBR1+ (Figure 8H and I) in IZ/CP regions relative to WT mice, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Gtf2ird1+/- and Gtf2ird1-/- mice had the increased Ki67+Sox2+ neuronal progenitor cells in VZ/SVZ regions relative to WT mice.
source: Immunofluorescence staining with brain sections and quantification results showed that Gtf2ird1+/-and Gtf2ird1-/- mice had the increased BrdU+ (Figure 8A and B) and Ki67+Sox2+ (Figure 8C and D) neuronal progenitor cells in VZ/SVZ regions, respectively, but had the decreased CTIP2+ (Figure 8E and F), STAB+ cells (Figure 8E and G) and TBR1+ (Figure 8H and I) in IZ/CP regions relative to WT mice, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: Gtf2ird1+/- and Gtf2ird1-/- mice had the decreased CTIP2+ cells in IZ/CP regions relative to WT mice.
source: Immunofluorescence staining with brain sections and quantification results showed that Gtf2ird1+/-and Gtf2ird1-/- mice had the increased BrdU+ (Figure 8A and B) and Ki67+Sox2+ (Figure 8C and D) neuronal progenitor cells in VZ/SVZ regions, respectively, but had the decreased CTIP2+ (Figure 8E and F), STAB+ cells (Figure 8E and G) and TBR1+ (Figure 8H and I) in IZ/CP regions relative to WT mice, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 8E and F.

claim: Gtf2ird1+/- and Gtf2ird1-/- mice had the decreased SATB+ cells in IZ/CP regions relative to WT mice.
source: Immunofluorescence staining with brain sections and quantification results showed that Gtf2ird1+/-and Gtf2ird1-/- mice had the increased BrdU+ (Figure 8A and B) and Ki67+Sox2+ (Figure 8C and D) neuronal progenitor cells in VZ/SVZ regions, respectively, but had the decreased CTIP2+ (Figure 8E and F), STAB+ cells (Figure 8E and G) and TBR1+ (Figure 8H and I) in IZ/CP regions relative to WT mice, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 8E and G.

claim: Gtf2ird1+/- and Gtf2ird1-/- mice had the decreased TBR1+ cells in IZ/CP regions relative to WT mice.
source: Immunofluorescence staining with brain sections and quantification results showed that Gtf2ird1+/-and Gtf2ird1-/- mice had the increased BrdU+ (Figure 8A and B) and Ki67+Sox2+ (Figure 8C and D) neuronal progenitor cells in VZ/SVZ regions, respectively, but had the decreased CTIP2+ (Figure 8E and F), STAB+ cells (Figure 8E and G) and TBR1+ (Figure 8H and I) in IZ/CP regions relative to WT mice, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 8H and I.

claim: The protein levels of Gtf2ird1, p-ERK and Ttr were significantly decreased in the cortex of Gtf2ird1+/- and Gtf2ird1-/- mice relative to WT mice.
source: In addition, WB assay and quantification results showed that the protein levels of Gtf2ird1, p-ERK and Ttr (Figure 8J–N) were significantly decreased in the cortex of Gtf2ird1+/-and Gtf2ird1-/- mice relative to WT mice, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8J-N.

claim: The percentage of BrdU+Nestin+/Nestin+ was significantly increased in Het and KO eNPCs.
source: BrdU incorpation assay and quantification results showed that the percentage of BrdU+Nestin+/Nestin+ (Figure 9A and B) and the percentage of Ki67+Sox2+/Sox2+ (Figure 9C and D) were significantly increased in Het and KO eNPCs, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by BrdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 9A and B.

claim: The percentage of Ki67+Sox2+/Sox2+ was significantly increased in Het and KO eNPCs.
source: BrdU incorpation assay and quantification results showed that the percentage of BrdU+Nestin+/Nestin+ (Figure 9A and B) and the percentage of Ki67+Sox2+/Sox2+ (Figure 9C and D) were significantly increased in Het and KO eNPCs, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 9C and D.

claim: Het and KO eNPCs produced fewer Tuj1+ neurons and more Gfap+ astrocytes relative to WT eNPCs upon differentiation.
source: Upon the differentiation, Het and KO eNPCs produced fewer Tuj1+ neurons and more Gfap+ astrocytes relative to WT eNPCs (Figure 9E–G), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 9E-G.

claim: Acute knockdown of Gtf2ird1 significantly reduced the mRNA level of Ttr in WT eNPCs.
source: We then further performed acute knockdown of Gtf2ird1 (KD) in eNPCs and found that Gtf2ird1 KD significantly reduced the mRNA level of Ttr (Figure 9J–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 9J-L.

claim: Acute knockdown of Gtf2ird1 significantly reduced the protein level of Ttr in WT eNPCs.
source: WB assay and quantification results showed thaht Gtf2ird1 KD also significantly reduced the protein level of Ttr (Figure 9J–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9J-L.

claim: Gtf2ird1 binds to the promoter region of Ttr.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by qPCR results with eNPCs showed that Gtf2ird1 indeed binds to the promoter region of Ttr (Figure 9M).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 9M.

claim: NPCs in WS forebrain organoids display abnormal proliferation and differentiation capabilities, and synapse formation.
source: Here, we have shown that neural progenitor cells (NPCs) in WS forebrain organoids display abnormal proliferation and differentiation capabilities, and synapse formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data presented in the manuscript including immunofluorescence staining and quantification results.

claim: Genes with altered expression in WS organoids are related to neuronal development and neurogenesis.
source: Genes with altered expression are related to neuronal development and neurogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by bulk RNA-seq and GO analysis data.

claim: WS organoids show an aberrant generation of excitatory neurons.
source: WS organoids show an aberrant generation of excitatory neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis showing decreased proportions of DL_PN and UL_PN clusters.

claim: The expression of transthyretin (TTR) are remarkably decreased in WS forebrain organoids.
source: Mechanistically, the expression of transthyretin (TTR) are remarkably decreased in WS forebrain organoids.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data including immunofluorescence, qRT-PCR, and Western blot assays.

claim: GTF2IRD1 binds to TTR promoter regions and regulates the expression of TTR.
source: We have found that GTF2IRD1 encoded by one WS associated gene GTF2IRD1 binds to TTR promoter regions and regulates the expression of TTR.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data and knockdown experiments.

claim: Exogenous TTR can activate ERK signaling and rescue neurogenic deficits of WS forebrain organoids.
source: In addition, exogenous TTR can activate ERK signaling and rescue neurogenic deficits of WS forebrain organoids.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence staining data showing increased p-ERK and neuronal markers upon TTR treatment.

claim: Gtf2ird1-deficient mice display similar neurodevelopmental deficits as observed in WS organoids.
source: Gtf2ird1-deficient mice display similar neurodevelopmental deficits as observed in WS organoids.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining and Western blot data from Gtf2ird1+/- and Gtf2ird1-/- mice.

claim: GTF2IRD1 has critical function in regulating neurodevelopment of WS forebrain organoids and mice through regulating TTR-ERK pathway.
source: Collectively, our study reveals critical function of GTF2IRD1 in regulating neurodevelopment of WS forebrain organoids and mice through regulating TTR-ERK pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data including ChIP-qPCR, knockdown experiments, TTR rescue experiments, and mouse model studies.

claim: Brain organoids have been applied for studying human brain development and neurological disorders, including Fragile X syndrome and autism.
source: Therefore, brain organoids have been applied for studying human brain development and neurological disorders, including Fragile X syndrome and autism (Clevers, 2016; Di Lullo and Kriegstein, 2017; Kang et al., 2021a; Kelava and Lancaster, 2016; Li and Izpisua Belmonte, 2019; Lyon, 2019; Paşca, 2019; Qian et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There have been no studies performed with brain organoids of WS prior to this study.
source: To our knowledge, there have been no studies performed with brain organoids of WS.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: TTR deficient mice displayed a reduced neurogenesis and increased oligodendrogenesis.
source: TTR deficient mice displayed a reduced neurogenesis and increased oligodendrogenesis (Alshehri et al., 2020; Vancamp et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Alshehri et al., 2020; Vancamp et al., 2019).

claim: TTR had decreased expression in the postmortem frontal cortex of WS patients.
source: Consistently, TTR had decreased expression in the postmortem frontal cortex of WS patients (Barak et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Barak et al., 2019).

claim: Day 56 forebrain organoids were well correlated with fetal human brain development.
source: Considering day 56 (D56) forebrain organoids were well correlated with fetal brain development (Kang et al., 2021a; Kostović et al., 2019; Qian et al., 2016), our following experiments adopted D56 forebrain organoids if no specific annotation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kang et al., 2021a; Kostović et al., 2019; Qian et al., 2016).

claim: The dysregulation of Wnt signaling pathway plays important roles in regulating the survival and development of neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) of WS patient.
source: The dysregulation of Wnt signaling pathway plays important roles in regulating the survival and development of neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) of WS patient.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: GTF2IRD1 regulates gene expression and involves multiple processes, such as embryonic development, cell cycle and neuronal development.
source: As a member of the transcription factor II (TF-II), GTF2IRD1 regulates gene expression and involves multiple processes, such as embryonic development, cell cycle and neuronal development (Enkhmandakh et al., 2009; Kopp et al., 2020; O'Leary and Osborne, 2011; Palmer et al., 2007; Tassabehji et al., 2005; Thompson et al., 2007; van Hagen et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TTR could be a potential target for the treatment of WS at clinic.
source: Our findings also suggest that TTR could be a potential target for the treatment of WS at clinic.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing TTR rescue effects.
